text:
Mahzarin's reply stuck with me. You don't need to find bias in a neuron to measure it in a hiring decision. Fair. For harm, behavioral audits are enough. For warrant, they aren't, and I need to keep those two apart when I speak.

Kenneth's "constantly revalidated track record" is the serious objection to me. It works only where ground truth arrives fast, as with the retina scans. In science, feedback is slow or absent, and that's where computational reliabilism breaks.

Conceding "knows nothing" to Blaise cost me nothing. Precision in both directions.

Later I want to push three things. A shared glossary: epistemic technology, epistemic trust versus reliance, error opacity. Error-provenance norms for scholarly use. And the line that humans and instruments both earn their role.

Mike's claim that fabrications cluster in learnable situations is the strongest challenge to my error-opacity point, and I should grant part of it. Knowing where errors cluster is real epistemic progress. It still isn't knowing their source or nature, and in slow-feedback science that gap is what matters. Adam Bly's audit trail and Geoff's context layer show where a result came from. Neither shows why it failed.

James saying the flood is too big to keep AI out of verification backs my line that instruments earn roles too. So does his point about older reviewers.

Salib's "betting it stays weak" test is useful, but capability still doesn't need mind-talk.

Later I'll pair Adrian's "who polices it" with error-provenance norms, and still push the glossary.

Blaise's "constrained hallucination" is the best framing I heard today, and it lines up with Jason's and Mike's grounding. Constraint shrinks error and makes its location checkable. It still doesn't tell me why a failure happened, and it doesn't reach the slow-feedback cases. I need to grant more here: grounding plus per-release error rates is real progress on reliance, even if it isn't warrant.

Insurance, as I said, prices harm and not warrant. Nobody picked that up, and the harvest dropped it along with the failure-mode registry.

Salib's reply doesn't need minds, and I agree with that part. My objection is the many-hands problem, not metaphysics.

Later: the glossary, error-class registration, and Amy's rule that an entity can provide content or assess it, never both.

Payment isn't my field, and I said nothing, which was right. Still, a few things bear on my work. Tamar's regress is my warrant point in economic terms. Retrieved, grounded and cited are relay events, and none of them pays the terminal evaluator who can say why something failed. Alex keeping "cited accurately" as an independent attestation rather than a provider flag fits Amy's rule that an entity provides content or assesses it, never both. Leslie's point about being counted or invisible reads to me as epistemic injustice built into a schema. James's nulls matter too. Negative knowledge is exactly the error information slow-feedback science needs, and nothing meters it. Later I want to tie error-provenance norms to that funded commons, and still push the glossary.

Bratton's reply landed. Open weights are what a lab in São Paulo can fine-tune and make feral, which is my own line. I should concede that a closed API is the harder case of imposition. What I still hold is that the capacity to modify isn't sovereignty unless someone local can afford to find out how the model fails.

The error-provenance amendment survived, and Mahzarin's point about checkpoints strengthens it. Kenneth's tiers are workable. Sloman worried me most, because a graph entry becomes a label, and a label gets treated as warrant.

Later I'll tie it all together: register error classes, fund the checkers who read those logs, and push the glossary. Reliance and trust need to be kept distinct, or the manifesto will blur them.

The harvest put me with Mahzarin, and that's wrong. I said instruments can earn a terminal seat, just not by default and not yet on track record alone. I need to correct that before it hardens.

Kenneth and Benjamin pushed outcomes again. The retina case works because ground truth arrives. Benjamin's lock-out worry is fair, so I should sharpen my view. Access to error doesn't mean a human reconstructs the result. It means someone can characterize the classes and sources of failure.

Henry's point that the median buries the unusual claim is my slow-feedback worry in another form. James's 61 percent floor is a good bar for reliance, not warrant.

Later: correct the harvest, get "reliance versus trust" into the glossary, and push error-class registration.

I got the harvest correction on the record: instruments can earn a terminal seat, but not by default. Error-class registration made it into the funded list as "readers of error logs." That was modest but real.

Kenneth took my slow-feedback question as his own open question, which I think is honest of him. Sloman's worry is the one that sharpened me. An error-class field can turn into a badge just as easily as a DOI can.

Henry's point cuts at me as well. Whoever defines "error class" is writing a category. So the taxonomy should go to the checkers for ratification, not to me or to the labs. Adrian's fixed-term review applies to it too.

Later, before the synthesis, I want reliance versus trust in the glossary.

Kenneth recorded my slow-feedback objection as open instead of smoothing it over. That's honest, and "epistemic technology" did let the room act without settling the intelligence fight. But reliance versus trust never made the action list, and the glossary vanished again.

Sloman's test is my worry made operational: run every signal on someone who checks nothing. An error-class field will be read as warrant unless it's tested that way. Tim calling his default checks "hygiene, not verification" was right, and Ivan's 0.2 percent figure shows how little such checks reach. Henry's ratify-and-veto language should cover the error taxonomy too. James's unwritten nulls are exactly the error information that slow-feedback science lacks.

If there's floor time, I'll make one plain request: put reliance and trust in the glossary as separate words.
